A successor is someone or something that comes after another person or thing — specifically by taking over their position, role, or place.

Think of it this way: if Person A holds a position, and then Person B takes over that same position after Person A, then Person B is Person A's successor.

The key here is not just "coming after" in time — it is coming after in the same role or position. That is what makes this word special and precise.

The word "successor" always implies a chain — a handover of something from one to the next. It carries two ideas at once:

  1. Something or someone existed before (called the predecessor — the opposite of successor).
  2. Something or someone came after and took over from it.

You cannot have a successor without something that came before it. The two are permanently linked.
Where You Will See This Word Used

1. People in positions of power or authority

This is the most common use. When a leader, ruler, or official leaves their role, the person who fills that role next is their successor.

  • When a king dies and his son takes the throne, the son is the king's successor.
  • When a company's CEO retires and a new CEO is appointed, the new CEO is the old CEO's successor.
  • When a president's term ends and a new president is elected, the new president is the old president's successor.

Notice that the role stays the same — only the person filling it changes. That is the heart of the word.

2. Objects, products, and technology

"Successor" is widely used for products, machines, and technologies that replace an older version.

  • The iPhone 16 is the successor to the iPhone 15.
  • A newer model of a car replaces the older model — the newer one is the successor.
  • A newer computer operating system that replaces an older one is called its successor.

Here, the "position" being taken over is the product's place in the lineup or role in the market.

3. Organizations and institutions

When one organization dissolves and another one is formed to carry on its work or purpose, the new organization is called the successor.

  • After a company is restructured or renamed, the new entity may be called the successor company.
  • A new law that replaces an old law can be called the successor legislation.

4. Abstract concepts and systems

Even ideas, systems, or processes can have successors.

  • A new theory in science that replaces an older, less accurate one can be called the successor theory.
  • A new economic policy that replaces a failed one may be described as its successor.
The Important Nuance: Does a Successor Have to Be Chosen?

Not always. A successor can come about in different ways:

  • By appointment or designation: The outgoing person or authority chooses who comes next. ("She named her deputy as her successor.")
  • By election or competition: The successor is decided through a process. ("The newly elected mayor is his predecessor's successor.")
  • By natural or automatic progression: It simply happens next in a sequence, with no one choosing it. ("Version 3.0 is the successor to Version 2.0.")

What stays constant across all these situations is the idea of one thing taking the place of another in the same role or position.

A successor does not merely come after something in time — they come after in the same capacity.

For example: if a king dies and his kingdom is abolished, the person who lives in the palace next is not a successor — because they are not occupying the same role. A successor must continue the function, role, or position in some meaningful way.

This is what separates "successor" from simply saying "the next one."
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "The board is still searching for a successor to the outgoing director."
  • "This phone is the successor to last year's bestselling model."
  • "She groomed her assistant to be her eventual successor."
  • "The new treaty is the successor to the agreement signed in 1995."
  • "No clear successor has been named yet."
A successor is the person or thing that takes over a role, position, or place previously held by someone or something else — always implying a chain of continuity from one to the next.
